title: Why your WordPress website is slow (and how to speed it up)

content.imageAlt: WordPress dashboard showing the list of installed plugins
content.excerpt: Page builders, too many plugins, heavy images and the wrong hosting: the most common causes, in order of impact, and what to do about each one.
content.lead: WordPress isn’t slow by nature: it gets slow when it’s weighed down. The good news is that the causes are nearly always the same, and in most cases you can improve things a lot without rebuilding the website. Here they are, in order of impact.
content.text:
## First things first: measure

Open PageSpeed Insights, enter the address of your homepage and one or two key pages, and look at the **mobile** results. Note down the scores and the Core Web Vitals: you’ll need them to see whether your fixes are working.

## Heavy page builders

Page builders let you create pages by dragging blocks around, but they often load a lot of code even where it isn’t needed. If your website is built with a heavy builder, sometimes the best fix is to slim down your most important pages or rebuild them with native blocks.

## Too many plugins (or the wrong ones)

It’s not just the number that counts: it’s what they do. One plugin that loads scripts and styles on every page weighs more than ten lightweight ones.

- remove the ones you no longer use;
- replace plugins that do the same job;
- check which ones load files on every page even when they’re not needed.

## Heavy images

This is the most common cause of a slow website. Multi-megabyte photos uploaded straight from the camera slow everything down.

- use modern formats like **WebP** or AVIF;
- upload images at the size they’re actually displayed;
- turn on lazy loading for images below the first screen.

## Hosting and caching

Cheap shared hosting crammed with hundreds of websites responds slowly, and no amount of optimization fully makes up for it. Alongside decent hosting you need properly configured **caching**, file compression and, if your audience is international, a CDN.

## Third-party scripts

Chat widgets, maps, videos, ad pixels, cookie banners, review widgets: every external service adds code to download and run. You don’t have to remove them, but load them **only when they’re needed**: the map only when the visitor scrolls to it, say, or the video only when they press play.

## Fonts and the database

Too many fonts, or fonts loaded from external services, delay text from appearing: stick to a few weights, hosted on your own server. And a database stuffed with revisions, drafts and data from uninstalled plugins slows down the dashboard and sometimes the website: a regular clean-up helps.

## After the fixes

Run the same measurements on the same pages again. Lighthouse will show the improvements straight away; the real-world visitor data Google uses for Core Web Vitals will update over a few weeks. And to keep your website fast over time, follow one simple rule: **weigh up every new plugin or service for its performance cost too**.
